questions.q: Why does /usr/bin/passwd need the setuid bit?
options: So any user can delete the passwd binary
So the program runs with root's privileges, letting an ordinary user update their own entry in the root-only /etc/shadow
So the program always runs faster
Setuid has no real effect on executables
questions.explain: setuid makes the program run as its owner (root), not as the calling user, which is the only way an unprivileged user can modify the root-only /etc/shadow file through passwd.

questions.q: What does setting setgid on a directory actually do?
options: It prevents anyone from writing to the directory
New files and subdirectories created inside automatically inherit the directory's group, instead of the creator's primary group
It makes the directory executable by root only
It is identical in effect to the sticky bit
questions.explain: setgid on a directory causes new content created inside to inherit the directory's group ownership, which is what makes shared team directories work consistently across different users' primary groups.

questions.q: What problem does the sticky bit solve on a directory like /tmp?
options: It stops any new files from being created in the directory
It prevents users from reading each other's files
It stops one user from deleting or renaming another user's files, even though the directory itself is writable by everyone
It automatically deletes files after 24 hours
questions.explain: The sticky bit restricts deletion/renaming inside a world-writable directory to each file's own owner (or root), which is exactly what a shared scratch space like /tmp needs.

questions.q: A file shows permissions as -rw-r--r--+ in `ls -l`. What does the trailing + indicate?
options: The file carries ACL entries beyond the standard owner/group/other permissions
The file is a symbolic link
questions.explain: A + appended after the normal permission string signals that the file has extra ACL entries, visible in full with getfacl.

questions.q: Which octal chmod value sets setuid, setgid, AND the sticky bit together, combined with rwxrwxrwx permissions?
questions.explain: The three special bits sum as a leading fourth digit: setuid=4000, setgid=2000, sticky=1000, totaling 7000; combined with 777 permissions that's chmod 7777.
